Fault Offsets

Tobias Stephan

2026-10-30

Source: vignettes/fault_offsets.qmd

This tutorial demonstrates how you can derive displacement components from fault slip.

The offset along a fault can be factorized into several components (Figure 1).

Get different components with trigonometry

Fault orientation (dip angle, dip direction), shortening direction, and horizontal throw

Knowing the horizontal throw (e.g. from plate motion parameters), the remaining components of the displacements along a given fault are as follows. The angle δ\delta between the direction of horizontal displacement (here assumed parallel to e3e_3) and the fault strike is

δ=|e3−(dip direction+90∘)| \delta = |e_3 - (\text{dip direction} + 90^{\circ})|

Slip components in the horizontal plane:

fstrike slip=|cos⁡δ⋅fhorizontal throw|fheave=fhorizontal throw2−fstrike slip2 \begin{aligned} f_\text{strike slip} &= |\cos{\delta} \cdot f_\text{horizontal throw}|\\ f_\text{heave} &= \sqrt{f_\text{horizontal throw}^2 - f_\text{strike slip}^2} \end{aligned}

Slip components in the vertical plane perpendicular to the strike of the fault:

fdip slip=fheavecos⁡(dip)fvertical throw=fdip slip2−fheave2 \begin{aligned} f_\text{dip slip} &= \frac{f_\text{heave}}{\cos{(\text{dip})}}\\ f_\text{vertical throw} &= \sqrt{f_\text{dip slip}^2 - f_\text{heave}^2} \end{aligned}

Slip components in the fault plane:

fnet slip=fstrike slip2+fdip slip2rake=arctan⁡(fdip slipfstrike slip) \begin{aligned} f_\text{net slip} &= \sqrt{f_\text{strike slip}^2 + f_\text{dip slip}^2}\\ \text{rake} &= \arctan{\left(\frac{f_\text{dip slip}}{f_\text{strike slip}}\right)} \end{aligned}

Thus, the rake angle describes the ratio between the dip slip and the strike slip component.

Knowing the vertical throw (e.g. from thermochronology or petrology), the (assumed) fault dip, and the direction and amount of horizontal offset, the strike of the fault is as follows:

fheave=fvertical throwtan⁡(dip)δ=arcsin⁡(fheavefhorizontal throw)strike=|e3−δ| \begin{aligned} f_\text{heave} &= \frac{f_\text{vertical throw}}{\tan{(\text{dip})}}\\ \delta &= \arcsin{\left(\frac{f_\text{heave}}{f_\text{horizontal throw}}\right)}\\ \text{strike} &= |e_3 - \delta| \end{aligned}

Knowing the vertical throw (e.g. from thermochronology or petrology), the fault strike (e.g. from geomorphology), and the direction and amount of horizontal offset, the dip of the fault is as follows:

δ=|e3−strike|fheave=fhorizontal throw⋅sin⁡δdip=arctan⁡(fvertical throwfheave) \begin{aligned} \delta &= |e_\text{3} - \text{strike}|\\ f_\text{heave} &= f_\text{horizontal throw} \cdot \sin{\delta}\\ \text{dip} &= \arctan{\left(\frac{f_\text{vertical throw}}{f_\text{heave}}\right)} \end{aligned}

Knowing the vertical throw (e.g. from thermochronology or petrology) and the fault’s dip and rake, the heave, the strike slip, the horizontal throw, and the net slip are as follows:

fdip slip=fvertical throwsin⁡(dip)fheave=fvertical throwtan⁡(dip)fstrike slip=fdip sliptan⁡(rake)fhorizontal throw=fstrike slip2+fheave2fnet slip=fdip slipsin⁡(rake) \begin{aligned} f_\text{dip slip} &= \frac{f_\text{vertical throw}}{\sin{(\text{dip})}}\\ f_\text{heave} &= \frac{f_\text{vertical throw}}{\tan{(\text{dip})}}\\ f_\text{strike slip} &= \frac{f_\text{dip slip}}{\tan{(\text{rake})}}\\ f_\text{horizontal throw} &= \sqrt{f_\text{strike slip}^2 + f_\text{heave}^2}\\ f_\text{net slip} &= \frac{f_\text{dip slip}}{\sin{(\text{rake})}} \end{aligned}

Fault displacement tensors

Each fault component is a vector describing its direction and length. For instance, the vector of the strike slip is:

f→strike slip=(‖fstrike slip‖00) \vec{f}_\text{strike slip} = \begin{pmatrix} \lVert f_\text{strike slip}\rVert \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}

Net slip vector

The net slip vector is the sum of the strike slip, heave, and vertical throw vectors:

f→net=(‖fstrike slip‖‖fheave‖‖fvertical throw‖) \vec{f}_\text{net} = \begin{pmatrix} \lVert f_\text{strike slip}\rVert \\ \lVert f_\text{heave}\rVert \\ \lVert f_\text{vertical throw}\rVert \end{pmatrix} 

fault_displacements(strikeslip = 2, verticalthrow = -5, heave = 3)

Principal displacement tensor

The eigenvalues of 𝖥ij\mathsf{F}_{ij} are the magnitudes of the heave, strike slip, and vertical throw components, and the corresponding eigenvectors {f→1,f→2,f→3}\{ \vec{f}_1, \vec{f}_2, \vec{f}_3 \} are mutually orthogonal unit vectors along these directions. In this principal frame the tensor is diagonal, i.e. the principal displacement tensor 𝖥𝔽\mathsf{F}_\mathbb{F}:

𝖥𝔽=[‖fheave‖000‖fstrike slip‖000‖fvertical throw‖] \mathsf{F}_{\mathbb{F}} = \begin{bmatrix} \lVert f_\text{heave}\rVert & 0 & 0\\ 0 & \lVert f_\text{strike slip}\rVert & 0\\ 0 & 0 & \lVert f_\text{vertical throw}\rVert\end{bmatrix}

The tensor 𝖥\mathsf{F} can also be defined by the magnitudes of the fault displacements:

Fu <- displacement_tensor(s = 2, v = -5, h = 3)
print(Fu)
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    3    0    0
[2,]    0    2    0
[3,]    0    0   -5
attr(,"class")
[1] "matrix"  "array"   "ftensor"

Orientation tensor

The fault orientation tensor is defined by the fault plane’s orientation (dip direction and dip angle) and the fault’s slip (direction and magnitude):

𝖥ij=[f11f12f13f21f22f23f31f32f33] \mathsf{F}_{ij} = \begin{bmatrix}f_{11} & f_{12} & f_{13}\\ f_{21} & f_{22} & f_{23}\\ f_{31} & f_{32} & f_{33}\end{bmatrix} 

Fg <- displacement_tensor(s = 2, v = -5, h = 3, dip_direction = 45)
print(Fg)
        [,1]      [,2] [,3]
[1,] 2.12132  1.414214    0
[2,] 2.12132 -1.414214    0
[3,] 0.00000  0.000000   -5
attr(,"class")
[1] "matrix"  "array"   "ftensor"

From principal displacement tensor to orientation tensor

Translate the origin of 𝖥𝔽\mathsf{F}_\mathbb{F} to the point of measurement and rotate it into the fault orientation, giving 𝖥𝔽𝔾\mathsf{F}_\mathbb{FG}:

displacement_tensor_decomposition(Fg, dip_direction = 45)
